Despite increased research and awareness since 2015 on
how better management can reduce soil threats, the
reality on the ground is that the deterioration of soils
continues at an alarming rate.
Overall, the global picture is sobering. Soil erosion
remains the most severe threat to soils worldwide. It is
also the most interconnected threat, stripping away
topsoil, reducing rooting depth, depleting nutrients and
carbon, limiting water infiltration, and increasing runoff,
thereby heightening the risk of floods and droughts. The
loss of soil organic carbon (SOC) is a major concern,
especially where deforestation, peatland drainage or
unsustainable practices have depleted organic matter.
Nutrient mismanagement, whether through overuse of
fertilizers leading to pollution or inadequate fertilizer
resulting in nutrient mining of soils is similarly
widespread. Particularly concerning is the continued
deterioration of soil biodiversity, which has emerged as
one of the most rapidly deteriorating soil threat globally.

As SWSR 2026 demonstrates, reversing global soil
World’s Soil Resources report 2026
degradation is an urgent priority requiring coordinated
(Click to enlarge)
and sustained action by governments, the private
sector, researchers, farmers and civil society. High-level
decision-makers are urged to recognize healthy soils as
strategic assets that underpin food security, water
security, climate change mitigation and adaptation,
biodiversity conservation, and resilient livelihoods.
Investing in soil health yields substantial
socioeconomic and environmental returns, far
outweighing the costs of inaction.
Action is needed at local, national, regional and
international levels, guided by five priorities:
1. strengthening soil governance and legal
frameworks;
2. promoting education, capacity development
and knowledge exchange;
3. improving soil monitoring through harmonized
soil data, indicators and assessment methods;
4. enhancing incentive frameworks to accelerate
the adoption of SSM; and
5. fostering inclusive, multidisciplinary and
multistakeholder decision-making.
Globally, we must shift from a mindset of soil exploitation
to one of soil stewardship. The knowledge, tools and
practices needed to protect and restore soils already
exist. The challenge is no longer knowing what needs to
be done, but acting with the urgency, ambition, long-
